title: {{NAME}} and the Match at the End of the Muddy World
moral: A team that lifts each other up will always outrun a team that pushes each other down.

pages.content:
The pitch had no name on any map, because no human cartographer had ever found it. It lay at the bottom of a long winding trail through Hawthorn Wood, accessible only to those who followed a badger, which is how {{NAME}} came to arrive, breathless and mud-splattered, at the most extraordinary football match he had ever witnessed.

The teams were entirely composed of animals. A heron played in goal at one end, standing on one leg with aristocratic patience. A pair of rabbits operated the centre circle with bewildering speed. Three foxes anchored the defence with cool, tactical efficiency. And at the heart of the action, a stout and exceptionally confident badger was running the midfield with the authority of someone who had invented the sport themselves.

The ball was bright white with black patches, standard in every respect, except that it appeared to do exactly what each player intended, which is something footballs do not always agree to.

{{NAME}} stood at the treeline with mud up to his ankles and his mouth open. The badger looked up from the centre spot, clocked him with one sharp glance, and pointed a broad paw at the empty left-wing position.

pages.content:
The badger's name was Marta, which she informed {{NAME}} at enormous speed while trotting alongside him to the left-wing position. She spoke the way she played: direct, fast, and with no space for unnecessary pauses.

'You're late, you'll play wide left, don't cut inside before the third marker, the hare on the other team is faster than she looks, and if a rabbit passes to you it means they trust you so do not waste it.'

{{NAME}}'s head was spinning. He looked out across the pitch: the opposing team was setting up a new attack, seven animals working with sharp, practised coordination. The opposing striker was a young vixen with a low centre of gravity and an expression of absolute focus. She was extremely fast. Marta had not exaggerated about that.

Then the ball came to {{NAME}}'s feet, a perfect rolling pass from the smaller of the two rabbits. It landed exactly where his boot was waiting, as though it had been aimed at him all his life. His face transformed: wide eyes, rising grin, certainty blooming from his chest outward.

pages.content:
The second half was chaos of the very best kind. {{NAME}} had played football in parks and playgrounds and patchy school fields, but he had never played at this pace, with these teammates. The rabbits were everywhere at once. The foxes defended as if reading minds. The heron in goal moved once, twice, with balletic precision, and stopped two shots that should have been unstoppable.

But it was {{NAME}}'s run in the seventy-third minute that the animals would talk about afterward. Marta had the ball deep and under pressure. Without looking she rolled it into the space {{NAME}} was already running into, and he took it at full stride, cut past the opposing fox defender with a step-over his left foot invented on the spot, and drove the ball low and hard toward the near post.

The vixen goalkeeper dived. The ball skimmed under her reaching paws by the width of a whisker.

Marta was beside him before he had finished celebrating, her broad paw on his back, propelling him forward in the direction of the centre circle with no time wasted on sentiment. 'Again,' she said simply. But her eyes were bright with fierce satisfaction.

pages.content:
Two minutes from time, the score was level. The opposing team had equalised with a brilliant header from a surprisingly aerial stoat, and now the forest pitch was absolutely silent except for the sound of everyone breathing hard.

The corner came to {{NAME}}. He controlled it on his chest, turned, and found three opponents surrounding him. He had one second. The rabbits were screaming for the ball but the angles were wrong. Marta was ten metres away, unmarked, in the perfect position, but Marta had already scored twice and there were animals on his team who had not scored all game.

He looked left. The heron, having come up for this last corner, stood unmarked at the far post. Their eyes met across the penalty area. {{NAME}} threaded the pass. The heron did not move her body. She simply extended one extraordinary wing and deflected the ball with immaculate control into the top corner.

The clearing erupted. The trees shook with noise. Every animal on the pitch was in motion, a blur of fur and feathers and golden light. The heron stood perfectly still in the chaos, one wing raised, expression composed, and inclined her long neck toward {{NAME}} in a slow, formal bow.

pages.content:
After the final whistle, the forest clearing settled into the kind of comfortable peace that comes after a great shared effort. The animals sprawled in the grass, panting and satisfied. The rabbits had disappeared up a nearby bank and returned with armfuls of berries, which they distributed with brisk, democratic efficiency.

{{NAME}} sat with his back against a broad oak root, yellow boots crossed in front of him, sharing berries with Marta. The heron had waded into the small stream at the clearing's edge and stood there with the contentment of someone who had done everything they intended to do today.

Marta did not say much. She ate berries. She watched the heron. She nudged {{NAME}}'s arm once with her broad, solid head. He leaned into it. They stayed like that as the light went golden and slow.

His eyelids drooped. The forest was full of small sounds: wind, water, creatures settling into the dusk. Tomorrow the pitch would be here. Tomorrow there might be a rematch.

Goodnight, number seven. Sleep deeply, and wonder which position Marta might play you in next time.
